howToCheck.machine: Compute line height divided by font size for paragraphs and flag values below the Catalog setting. Inject the four WCAG 1.4.12 override values and detect clipped or overlapping text. Flag text-align: justify and negative letter-spacing on body text.
howToCheck.human: Apply a text-spacing bookmarklet and read each page; nothing should be cut off or overlap.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing (Level AA) requires that content survive the four overrides; WCAG 1.4.8 (Level AAA) asks for at least space-and-a-half line spacing and no justification. Research is narrower: Ling and van Schaik (2007) found better accuracy and speed in visual search with wider line spacing and with left-aligned text; Rello and colleagues (2016) found little effect of line spacing except at the extremes; Zorzi and colleagues (2012, 74 children with dyslexia) found that extra-large letter spacing improved reading at once; the W3C explanation cites McLeish (2007) for readers with low vision. A study of normally sighted adults (Chung 2002, listed by W3C; its result is recalled from memory) found no gain beyond standard spacing.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.12 Text Spacing, Level AA.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.12: Text Spacing (lists McLeish 2007, Chung 2002 and 2012, Zorzi et al. 2012).
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.8: Visual Presentation.
Ling, J., & van Schaik, P. (2007). The influence of line spacing and text alignment on visual search of web pages. Displays, 28(2), 60-67.
Zorzi, M., et al. (2012). Extra-large letter spacing improves reading in dyslexia. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(28), 11455-11459.

entries.caveats: WCAG 1.4.12 does not require authors to use the override values; it requires that nothing breaks when a reader applies them. Print typesetters justify successfully with hyphenation and fine control that browsers apply unevenly. The spacing benefit for dyslexia was shown in children with spacing well above the default.

entries.principle: All capitals: fine for short labels, slower for running text
entries.claim: Continuous text in capitals reads somewhat more slowly than mixed-case text and takes more space, while short capitalised labels are not a problem and capitals can even be more legible at very small sizes. The popular explanation that people read by 'word shape' is not supported.
entries.mechanism: Readers recognise words through their letters, processed in parallel, not through the outline of the word. Capitals are bigger, which helps when size is the limit, but people have far less practice with all-capital text, and capitals put fewer words within one glance.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — sentence case keeps long text at normal reading speed
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited sources
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Use sentence case for anything longer than a few words.
Keep capitals for short labels such as tags, overlines and small buttons, and add a little letter spacing (typographic convention).
Never set paragraphs, error messages or legal text in capitals.
Produce capitals with CSS text-transform and keep the source text in normal case (practitioner convention).
antiPatterns: Paragraphs or long headings in capitals.
Warnings in capitals, which read as shouting.
Capitals justified by the claim that they are 'more readable', or banned by the claim that 'word shape' is lost.

howToCheck.machine: Find text with text-transform: uppercase or text typed in capitals. Flag instances longer than a Catalog-set number of words and report their letter spacing.
howToCheck.human: Read each capitalised string aloud; if it is a sentence, change it to sentence case.

evidence.strengthNote: The evidence is mixed and partly old. Larson (2004), a reading psychologist at Microsoft, reviews word-recognition research and concludes that the word-shape model is no longer viable; he puts the lower-case speed advantage at 5 to 10%. Secondary sources cite Tinker (1955) for about 13% slower reading of capitals in print. Arditi and Cho (2007, Vision Research) found capitals more legible than other case styles when size is the limit, especially for readers with low vision. No modern large-sample screen study was found.

sources.citation: Larson, K. (2004). The science of word recognition. Microsoft Typography.
Arditi, A., & Cho, J. (2007). Letter case and text legibility in normal and low vision. Vision Research, 47(19), 2499-2505.

entries.caveats: The slowdown estimates come from mid-twentieth-century print studies with long reading sessions. Practice matters: people who often read capitals read them well.

entries.principle: Light versus dark backgrounds
entries.claim: For reading and proofreading, dark text on a light background gives better performance than light text on a dark background for people with normal vision, young and old. The claim that dark mode reduces eye strain has little empirical support.
entries.mechanism: A bright background makes the pupil smaller. A smaller pupil produces a sharper image on the retina, which helps with fine detail such as small text. The advantage is attributed to the higher luminance of the light display.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a light background makes small text slightly easier to resolve
effects.satisfaction: mixed — many people prefer dark themes, and preference is a valid reason to offer one
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; polarity should not change how an interface is understood

designMoves: Use a light theme as the default for reading-heavy products and for small text.
Offer a dark theme as a user choice and follow the operating-system setting (the prefers-color-scheme media query).
Check contrast separately in each theme.
Do not claim in product copy that the dark theme protects the eyes.
antiPatterns: A dark-only product for long-form reading.
A dark theme produced by inverting colours without rechecking contrast.
Small, thin, light text on a dark background.

howToCheck.machine: Detect polarity from background and text luminance. If the Prescription asks for two themes, emulate prefers-color-scheme light and dark and run the contrast checks in both.
howToCheck.human: Read a long passage in each theme in a bright room and in a dim room.

evidence.strengthNote: Piepenbrock, Mayr, Mund and Buchner (2013, Ergonomics) measured visual acuity and proofreading in younger and older adults, found an advantage for dark-on-light in both groups, and recommend it for all ages. Piepenbrock's 2014 dissertation ties the effect to pupil size and reports that it is strongest for fine detail. Earlier work from the same laboratory (Buchner and Baumgartner 2007, recalled from memory) agrees. On eye strain, the search found only statements that empirical research is limited. Dark themes do save energy on OLED screens, but mostly at high brightness (secondary source, not verified).

sources.citation: Piepenbrock, C., Mayr, S., Mund, I., & Buchner, A. (2013). Positive display polarity is advantageous for both younger and older adults. Ergonomics, 56(7), 1116-1124.
Piepenbrock, C. (2014). Doctoral dissertation on display polarity, pupil size and legibility, Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf.
Buchner, A., & Baumgartner, N. (2007). Text-background polarity affects performance irrespective of ambient illumination and colour contrast. Ergonomics, 50(7), 1036-1063.

entries.caveats: Some readers with low vision or light sensitivity read better on dark backgrounds, so a choice serves accessibility. The measured advantage is modest and comes from laboratory tasks with small text. In dark surroundings a bright screen causes glare, which is a comfort reason for a dark theme and is separate from legibility.

entries.principle: No typeface is the most readable for everyone
entries.claim: Serifs make no meaningful difference to legibility, and in a large study each reader's fastest typeface was different and was not reliably the one they preferred.
entries.mechanism: Legibility depends on letter size, spacing, stroke weight and how distinct similar letters are, and readers differ in eyesight and familiarity. Serifs add a little space between letters, which can explain the small differences that some studies report.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — a well-spaced typeface with distinct letters lowers effort; the serif question does not matter
effects.satisfaction: mixed — preference and speed did not coincide
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; typeface choice should not change how an interface is understood

designMoves: Choose body typefaces for generous x-height, open letter shapes, even spacing and letters that cannot be confused (capital I, lowercase l and the digit 1; capital O and zero).
Do not decide between serif and sans-serif on legibility grounds.
Use regular or heavier weights for body text.
Use relative units and avoid forcing font declarations, so that readers' own font settings work.
Where reading is the product, let the reader choose among several typefaces.
antiPatterns: Marketing a typeface as 'scientifically the most readable'.
Light or hairline weights for body text.
Display or condensed faces for paragraphs.

howToCheck.machine: Report body font family, weight (flag below 400) and x-height ratio. Render the easily confused characters in the interface typeface and compare the bitmaps to flag near-identical glyphs. Check that sizes use relative units.
howToCheck.human: Have several people of different ages read a real page of content in the candidate typefaces.

evidence.strengthNote: Arditi and Cho (2005, Vision Research) compared typefaces that differed only in serifs and found no meaningful legibility difference; a small serif effect was attributed to added letter spacing. Wallace and colleagues (2022, ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction) tested several hundred crowdsourced readers: reading speed was 35% higher in each person's fastest font than in their slowest, with no loss of comprehension, and preference did not reliably predict speed.

sources.citation: Arditi, A., & Cho, J. (2005). Serifs and font legibility. Vision Research, 45(23), 2926-2933.

Wallace, S., Bylinskii, Z., Dobres, J., Kerr, B., Berlow, S., Treitman, R., Kumawat, N., Arpin, K., Miller, D. B., Huang, J., & Sawyer, B. D. (2022). Towards individuated reading experiences: Different fonts increase reading speed for different individuals. ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 29(4), Article 38.

entries.caveats: The 35% figure is the spread between each person's best and worst font among those tested, not the gain from leaving a default. All tested fonts were common, well-made text faces; a poorly made font can still be worse for everyone.

entries.principle: Dyslexia fonts do not help; spacing sometimes does
entries.claim: Typefaces designed for dyslexia have not improved reading speed or accuracy in controlled studies. What helps some readers with dyslexia is wider spacing between letters, which works in ordinary typefaces.
entries.mechanism: The special typefaces change letter shapes. Many readers with dyslexia are unusually affected by crowding, the interference between neighbouring letters, and crowding depends on spacing and not on shape.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the fonts themselves show no measured benefit; spacing options lower effort for some readers
effects.satisfaction: mixed — some readers like these fonts even without a measured gain
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Do not present a dyslexia font as an accessibility feature.
Use a clear, familiar typeface with adequate default spacing.
Make layouts survive user changes to spacing and typeface (see spacing-and-justification).
Where reading is the product, offer spacing and typeface controls and let readers choose.
antiPatterns: A 'dyslexia-friendly' toggle that only swaps the font.
Layouts that break when a reader increases letter spacing.
Claims that a font 'treats' or 'solves' dyslexia.

howToCheck.machine: Run the WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing override test. Check that a user stylesheet can replace the font family (no forced inline font declarations).
howToCheck.human: If a font toggle exists, ask what evidence supports it.

evidence.strengthNote: Kuster, van Weerdenburg, Gompel and Bosman (2018, Annals of Dyslexia) ran two experiments; the second included 102 children with dyslexia and 45 without, and the Dyslexie font neither helped nor hindered. Two further studies are recalled from memory and were not re-verified: Wery and Diliberto (2017) found no gain from OpenDyslexic, and Marinus and colleagues (2016) found that an apparent Dyslexie benefit vanished when spacing was matched. Zorzi and colleagues (2012) found that extra-large letter spacing improved reading in 74 children with dyslexia. The font developer's own site reports benefits; the independent studies do not.

sources.citation: Kuster, S. M., van Weerdenburg, M., Gompel, M., & Bosman, A. M. T. (2018). Dyslexie font does not benefit reading in children with or without dyslexia. Annals of Dyslexia, 68(1), 25-42.
Zorzi, M., et al. (2012). Extra-large letter spacing improves reading in dyslexia. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(28), 11455-11459.
Wery, J. J., & Diliberto, J. A. (2017). The effect of a specialized dyslexia font, OpenDyslexic, on reading rate and accuracy. Annals of Dyslexia, 67(2), 114-127.
Marinus, E., Mostard, M., Segers, E., Schubert, T. M., Madelaine, A., & Wheldall, K. (2016). A special font for people with dyslexia: Does it work and, if so, why? Dyslexia, 22(3), 233-244.

entries.caveats: Most studies tested children. A reader who likes a font may read more willingly, which has value even without a speed gain. The spacing benefit used spacing far above the default and has not been found in every later study (recalled from memory).

entries.principle: Typeface personality is real; hard-to-read type does not aid memory
entries.claim: People assign consistent personalities to typefaces, so type choice sets tone. Making text harder to read does not improve memory or learning, so body text should never trade legibility for tone.
entries.mechanism: Through exposure, people link letterform features with traits such as formal, friendly or technical. The 'disfluency' idea held that hard-to-read type forces deeper processing; pooled evidence shows no learning benefit.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — keeping body text plain avoids decoding effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — tone that matches the content is judged as more appropriate (survey evidence)
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Choose display type for tone and body type for legibility.
Confine expressive typefaces to short, large text such as headings and hero lines.
Set interface text, forms, tables and long reading in a plain, legible face.
Check the tone with a few people from the audience: ask them to describe the brand from a specimen.
Do not use hard-to-read styling to make people 'read carefully'.
antiPatterns: A script or display face for paragraphs or form fields.
Thin, low-contrast text chosen for elegance.
A 'memory-boosting' font.

howToCheck.machine: Report every font family and where it is used. Flag families that the Catalog classes as display or script when they are applied to paragraphs, inputs or table cells.
howToCheck.human: Show the type specimen to five people and collect three adjectives from each; compare with the intended tone.

evidence.strengthNote: Disfluency: Xie, Zhou and Liu (2018) meta-analysed 39 experiments from 25 articles (3,135 participants) and found a null effect of hard-to-read text on learning; Taylor and colleagues (2020, four experiments) and Geller and colleagues (2020, three preregistered experiments) found equal or worse memory with the Sans Forgetica font. Personality: Shaikh, Chaparro and Fox (2006) surveyed 561 people who rated 20 fonts on 15 adjective pairs and found that ratings followed the design family; this was a laboratory newsletter survey, not a journal article. Brumberger (2003) is the standard academic reference; only its existence was confirmed.

sources.citation: Xie, H., Zhou, Z., & Liu, Q. (2018). Null effects of perceptual disfluency on learning outcomes in a text-based educational context: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 745-771.
Taylor, A., Sanson, M., Burnell, R., Wade, K. A., & Garry, M. (2020). Disfluent difficulties are not desirable difficulties: The (lack of) effect of Sans Forgetica on memory. Memory, 28(7), 850-857.
Shaikh, A. D., Chaparro, B. S., & Fox, D. (2006). Perception of fonts: Perceived personality traits and uses. Usability News, 8(1).
Brumberger, E. R. (2003). The rhetoric of typography: The persona of typeface and text. Technical Communication, 50(2), 206-223.

entries.caveats: The personality ratings come from one country and one set of fonts; associations vary with culture and fashion. The first report of a disfluency benefit (2011) did not hold up in later work.

entries.principle: Align numbers and use equal-width digits in tables
entries.claim: Numbers that people compare down a column are easier to compare when every digit has the same width and the numbers line up on the right or on the decimal point. This is long-standing typographic and table-design practice; no controlled study was found.
entries.mechanism: With equal-width (tabular) digits, digits of the same place value stack in a vertical line, so size can be read from the length and position of the number. Proportional digits and centred numbers break that line (see alignment-continuity).

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — magnitude can be compared by position, without reading each number (argument from practice, not measured)
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — columns look ordered (argument from practice)

designMoves: Apply font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums to tables, price lists, timers and counters that update.
Right-align columns of quantities and give each column a consistent number of decimal places.
Left-align columns of text and align each header with its data.
Keep proportional digits for numbers inside running text.
Left-align identifiers such as phone numbers and reference codes, because they are not quantities.
antiPatterns: Centred numeric columns.
Mixed decimal places in one column.
A counter or timer that jitters because digit widths differ.

howToCheck.machine: For table cells whose content parses as a number, assert that font-variant-numeric includes tabular-nums or that the font has fixed-width digits, that alignment is right or end, and that decimal places are consistent within the column.
howToCheck.human: Scan a numeric column and check that the largest values can be picked out by length alone.

evidence.strengthNote: Craft guidance from typography and table-design authors (Bringhurst; Few), cited from memory and not verified in this search. No experiment that isolates tabular digits or right alignment was found. The supporting argument borrows from the alignment principle.

sources.citation: Bringhurst, R. (2012). The Elements of Typographic Style (4th ed.). Hartley & Marks.
Few, S. (2012). Show Me the Numbers: Designing Tables and Graphs to Enlighten (2nd ed.). Analytics Press.

entries.caveats: Some typefaces have tabular digits by default and some have none. Right alignment and decimal alignment are equivalent only when decimal places are consistent.

entries.principle: Text contrast: at least 4.5 to 1
entries.claim: Text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, or 3 to 1 for large text (WCAG 2.2, Level AA). Low-contrast text is the most common detectable accessibility failure on the web.
entries.mechanism: Reading depends on the light-dark difference between letters and background. Sensitivity to that difference falls with age and with many eye conditions. The W3C derived 4.5 from a baseline of 3 to 1 for normal vision, multiplied by 1.5 to cover the contrast-sensitivity loss associated with 20/40 acuity, which it describes as typical at about age 80.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — letters are resolved without strain, most of all for older readers and in glare
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the standard reports no satisfaction data
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; contrast decides whether text can be read, not how the interface is understood

designMoves: Give body text at least 4.5 to 1 contrast, and large text (18 point, or 14 point bold; about 24 and 18.5 CSS pixels) at least 3 to 1.
Apply the same floor to secondary text, placeholder text, links and text inside buttons.
For text on images or gradients, test the worst point under the text, or put a solid surface behind it.
Aim for 7 to 1 (Level AAA) for long reading.
Check every theme separately.
antiPatterns: Light grey text on white for hints, captions or timestamps.
White text on a light brand colour.
Text placed directly on a photograph.
Judging contrast by eye on a bright designer monitor.

howToCheck.machine: Compute the WCAG 2.x contrast ratio for every text node against its effective background (axe-core does this for solid backgrounds). For text over images or gradients, sample the pixels under the text and use the worst value. Include placeholder and link text. Repeat in each theme.
howToCheck.human: Read the page outdoors on a phone, and confirm the pairs that a script cannot resolve (text over images).

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3 and its explanation were read from the W3C source repository. The 3 to 1 baseline comes from older display standards (ISO 9241-3 and ANSI/HFES 100-1988); 7 to 1 at Level AAA is tied to about 20/80 acuity. Prevalence: the WebAIM Million 2026 analysis of one million home pages found low-contrast text on 83.9% of them, up from 79.1% in 2025 (figures from secondary reports of the study).

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), Level AA.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum).
WebAIM (2026). The WebAIM Million: The 2026 report on the accessibility of the top 1,000,000 home pages.

entries.caveats: The criterion exempts logos, decorative text and inactive controls. The WCAG 2 formula is a simple model: it ignores font weight and size beyond the large-text rule and is known to misjudge some dark colour pairs, so a passing pair can still be hard to read in a thin typeface. Passing an automated check covers only what the script could resolve.

entries.principle: Control boundaries, state indicators and focus must be visible
entries.claim: The visual parts needed to identify a control and its state, and the parts of a graphic needed to understand it, need at least 3 to 1 contrast against adjacent colours (WCAG 1.4.11, Level AA). Keyboard focus must be visible (2.4.7, AA) and must not be completely hidden by other content (2.4.11, AA).
entries.mechanism: A control that cannot be seen cannot be found. Faint boundaries vanish for people with low vision and for everyone in glare. People who use a keyboard track their position by the focus indicator, as mouse users track the pointer.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — controls and the current position are found without searching
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the standard reports no satisfaction data
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — fields look like fields and the current position is clear

designMoves: Give input borders, icon-only buttons and state marks (checked, selected, on or off) at least 3 to 1 contrast against what surrounds them.
Show a clear focus indicator on every interactive element; a ring 2 CSS pixels thick with a 3 to 1 change is the Level AAA benchmark (2.4.13).
Never remove the focus outline without providing a replacement.
Keep sticky headers, footers and banners from covering the focused element.
Give chart lines, bars and segments at least 3 to 1 contrast against the background.
antiPatterns: Pale grey input borders on a white page.
The declaration outline: none with no replacement focus style.
A toggle whose on and off states differ only by a slight tint.
A cookie banner or sticky footer that covers the focused field.

howToCheck.machine: Compute the contrast of control boundaries, icons and state indicators against adjacent colours and flag values under 3 to 1. Tab through every focusable element; compare screenshots of the focused and unfocused states, assert a visible difference, and report its thickness and contrast change. Assert that the focused element is not completely covered by another element.
howToCheck.human: Complete the main task with the keyboard alone and note any moment at which the current position is lost.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 Success Criteria 1.4.11, 2.4.7, 2.4.11 and 2.4.13 were read from the W3C source repository. The first three are Level AA; 2.4.13 Focus Appearance is Level AAA. The standard states requirements and reports no effect sizes.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.13 Focus Appearance, Level AAA.

entries.caveats: Criterion 1.4.11 exempts inactive controls and controls whose appearance the browser sets without author changes. It covers only the parts needed to identify the control; decorative edges are outside it.

entries.principle: Never use colour as the only signal
entries.claim: Colour must not be the only way to convey information, indicate an action or distinguish an element (WCAG 1.4.1, Level A). About 8% of men and about 0.4% of women of European descent have red-green colour-vision deficiency.
entries.mechanism: In the common forms of colour-vision deficiency one of the three cone types is missing or altered, so reds and greens look alike in hue while lightness differences stay visible. Older people and people with partial sight often see colour less well, and glare or a monochrome display removes it for everyone.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a second cue removes guessing for people who cannot use the colour
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the standard reports no satisfaction data
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — status and meaning are readable without relying on colour memory

designMoves: Pair colour with text, an icon, a pattern or a position for status, errors, required fields and chart series.
Mark links inside text with an underline or another non-colour cue.
Show an error with an icon and a text message, not only a red border.
Label chart series directly, and vary line style or marker shape.
Choose category colours that also differ in lightness.
antiPatterns: Red and green status dots with no label.
Required fields marked only by a coloured label.
Links that differ from the surrounding text only in hue.
A chart whose series can be told apart only through a colour legend.

howToCheck.machine: Render the page in greyscale and under simulated protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia. For each pair of states or categories, check for a non-colour difference (text, icon, shape, underline) or a lightness contrast of at least 3 to 1 between them. Flag links in body text without an underline or other cue, and error states shown by colour alone.
howToCheck.human: View the page in greyscale and try to read every status and chart.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.1 and its explanation were read from the W3C source repository; the explanation gives no prevalence figures. Prevalence comes from Birch (2012), a review in the Journal of the Optical Society of America A, as reported by secondary sources: about 8% of men and 0.4% of women of European descent, and about 4 to 6.5% of men of Chinese and Japanese ethnicity. Another review gives 0.5% for women.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color, Level A.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.1: Use of Color.
Birch, J. (2012). Worldwide prevalence of red-green color deficiency. Journal of the Optical Society of America A, 29(3), 313-320.

entries.caveats: The criterion does not discourage colour; it requires a second cue. A lightness difference of at least 3 to 1 between two colours counts as a second cue under the W3C explanation, but that is hard to combine with 4.5 to 1 text contrast, so a non-colour cue is safer. Colour-only distinction between visited and unvisited links is not a failure.

entries.principle: Lightness carries legibility; hue and chroma carry meaning and emphasis
entries.claim: Legibility comes from lightness difference; hue difference alone is unreliable. The 'lightness' number in HSL colour notation is not perceived lightness, so colour ramps should be built on a perceptual lightness scale and then verified with the contrast formula.
entries.mechanism: Fine detail such as letter shapes is resolved mainly through the light-dark channel of vision. In experiments, adding colour contrast to luminance contrast gave no extra reading speed, and readers with low vision read better with luminance contrast. HSL lightness is a calculation on screen values: a pure yellow and a pure blue with the same HSL lightness look very different in brightness.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — text and symbols stay legible for every viewer and on every screen
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited sources
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — evenly stepped ramps make hierarchy consistent across hues

designMoves: Make text differ from its background in lightness, whatever the two hues are.
Check each screen in greyscale; everything that must be read should survive.
Build tints and shades on a perceptual lightness axis (OKLCH or CIELAB) so that the same step looks equally light in every hue.
Use hue to name categories and states, and chroma (colourfulness) in small amounts for emphasis.
Verify every final text pair with the WCAG contrast ratio.
antiPatterns: Red text on a green background of similar lightness.
A palette built from fixed HSL lightness steps, in which the yellow step and the blue step differ greatly in brightness.
Saturated blue text on black.

howToCheck.machine: Convert every colour token to OKLCH. Check that each ramp is monotonic and roughly even in lightness and that the same step has similar lightness across hues. Render the page in greyscale and repeat the text-contrast check. Flag text and background pairs that differ mainly in hue.
howToCheck.human: Print or view the palette in greyscale and confirm that the step order is still visible.

evidence.strengthNote: Legge, Parish, Luebker and Wurm (1990, Journal of the Optical Society of America A) tested 8 normally sighted and 10 low-vision readers: high colour contrast alone can support fast reading in normal vision, combining it with luminance contrast adds nothing, and all low-vision readers read large text better with luminance contrast. The W3C explanation of the contrast criterion states that hue and saturation have minimal or no effect on legibility as assessed by reading performance. The statement that OKLCH lightness is perceptual while HSL lightness is not was read in MDN documentation. Building ramps in OKLCH is practitioner guidance (grade C); no study of its effect on users was found.

sources.citation: Legge, G. E., Parish, D. H., Luebker, A., & Wurm, L. H. (1990). Psychophysics of reading. XI. Comparing color contrast and luminance contrast. Journal of the Optical Society of America A, 7(10), 2002-2010.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum).
MDN Web Docs. oklch() CSS color function reference.

entries.caveats: Perceptual colour spaces are approximations; very saturated colours look brighter than their measured lightness. Equal OKLCH lightness does not guarantee an equal WCAG ratio, which is why the final check uses the WCAG formula. Normal readers can read text defined by strong hue contrast alone, so the rule protects robustness and low-vision readers; it does not describe a strict impossibility.

entries.principle: The same colour looks different on different backgrounds
entries.claim: A colour's appearance shifts away from its surroundings: a mid-grey looks lighter on black and darker on white. People therefore misjudge colour-coded values and fail to match the same colour across different backgrounds.
entries.mechanism: The visual system codes colour and lightness relative to the surrounding area and not as absolute values. This sharpens edges, and it biases the judgement of any patch by its neighbours.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — direct labels remove the need to match and judge colours
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — a colour that keeps one appearance keeps one meaning

designMoves: Do not ask people to match a swatch against a legend across different backgrounds; label the item directly.
Place colour-coded items on one uniform, neutral surface.
Check each brand and status colour on every surface on which it appears, and define a variant per surface or theme where needed.
Show the number as well wherever colour encodes a quantity.
antiPatterns: Status colours on rows with different tinted backgrounds.
One colour token assumed to look identical on light and dark surfaces.
A heat map with no value labels and no tooltip.

howToCheck.machine: List every background on which each semantic colour token is drawn. Flag tokens that appear on backgrounds of very different lightness without a per-surface variant. Flag charts that encode a quantity by colour with no labels or tooltips.
howToCheck.human: Place the same status chip on each surface side by side and judge whether it still reads as the same colour.

evidence.strengthNote: Simultaneous contrast is a textbook perceptual effect. Applied evidence is small and old: Ware (1988) tested 10 observers with five colour sequences on maps and found reading errors in the direction predicted by simultaneous contrast; Cleveland and McGill (1983) demonstrated a colour-caused illusion on a statistical map. No study of the effect's size in ordinary interfaces was found.

sources.citation: Ware, C. (1988). Color sequences for univariate maps: Theory, experiments and principles. IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications, 8(5), 41-49.
Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1983). A color-caused optical illusion on a statistical graph. The American Statistician, 37(2), 101-105.

entries.caveats: In ordinary interface work the shift is usually small; it matters most for data graphics, for brand-colour matching and for subtle status tints. In Ware's study a multi-hue spectrum scale gave the most accurate value reading, but such scales have other drawbacks (no natural order, colour-vision deficiency), so labels are the safer remedy.

entries.principle: Only a handful of colours work as category codes
entries.claim: People can tell apart at a glance only a small number of colours used as codes; older guidance says five to seven, and no firm universal limit exists. Small or thin marks need bigger colour differences than large areas.
entries.mechanism: Fast identification requires that each colour is clearly distinct from every other colour and easy to name. As the count rises, neighbours in colour space move closer together. Perceived colour difference also shrinks as a mark gets smaller or thinner.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer codes to learn and fewer trips to the legend
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — each colour keeps one clear meaning

designMoves: Keep a categorical palette to a handful of colours; beyond that, group categories, label them directly or use another channel such as position or shape.
Choose colours that have different names (blue, orange, green) and that also differ in lightness.
Use larger colour differences for thin lines, small dots and text than for filled areas.
Reserve a neutral colour for 'other' or inactive items.
antiPatterns: A legend with twelve colours.
Two shades of blue for two unrelated categories.
Tiny status dots that differ only by a subtle hue.

howToCheck.machine: Count the distinct categorical colours per chart, legend or status set and flag counts above the Catalog limit. Compute pairwise colour differences within the set, with and without simulated colour-vision deficiency, and flag pairs below the Catalog threshold; raise the threshold for small marks.
howToCheck.human: Cover the legend and ask a viewer to name the category of several marks.

evidence.strengthNote: Healey (1996, IEEE Visualization) ran target-identification experiments with 38 observers and proposed a method for choosing colours that stay rapidly identifiable; he quotes 'no more than five to seven colours' as an existing, partly anecdotal guideline, and his own numeric result was not confirmed here. Szafir (2018, IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics) used crowdsourced studies to show that perceived colour difference falls as marks get smaller and that elongated marks are easier to tell apart. The exact limit depends on the colours, the mark size, the background and the display.

sources.citation: Healey, C. G. (1996). Choosing effective colours for data visualization. Proceedings of IEEE Visualization 1996, 263-270.
Szafir, D. A. (2018). Modeling color difference for visualization design. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 24(1), 392-401.

entries.caveats: With labels and practice people handle more codes, as on a transit map. The limit concerns colours that must be identified without a label; it does not restrict decorative palettes.

entries.principle: Colour meanings are shared conventions, not universal laws
entries.claim: Colour-meaning associations are broadly similar across cultures but not identical, and colours that match the meaning of what they label make displays faster to read. Interface conventions such as red for errors work because they are learned and applied consistently.
entries.mechanism: People learn colour associations from the physical world and from language. When a colour agrees with the meaning of its label, recognition is faster; when it conflicts, the two compete.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a learned colour meaning is recognised without reading
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — states look the way people expect

designMoves: Reserve red for errors and destructive actions, green for success and amber for warnings, and keep each colour to one meaning across the product.
Do not use the error colour for emphasis or decoration.
If the brand colour is red, separate errors by icon, wording and placement.
Pair every semantic colour with an icon or text (see color-not-alone).
Check conventions for the target market before fixing a status palette.
antiPatterns: A red primary button for a harmless action beside red error text.
Green used for both 'selected' and 'success'.
Arbitrary colours for categories that have natural associations.

howToCheck.machine: Map colour tokens to roles. Flag the error-role colour on non-error elements, semantic colours with no accompanying icon or text, and two roles that share one hue.
howToCheck.human: Ask people from the target market what each status colour means to them, without showing labels.

evidence.strengthNote: Jonauskaite and colleagues (2020, Psychological Science) surveyed 4,598 people in 30 nations: colour-emotion association patterns were highly similar across nations (average similarity r = .88), yet nation still predicted associations, and nations closer in language or geography were more alike. Lin, Fortuna, Kulkarni, Stone and Heer (2013) found that colours matched to category meaning sped up chart reading compared with a default palette. Neither study tested interface status colours; the red, amber and green convention rests on practice.

sources.citation: Jonauskaite, D., et al. (2020). Universal patterns in color-emotion associations are further shaped by linguistic and geographic proximity. Psychological Science, 31(10), 1245-1260.
Lin, S., Fortuna, J., Kulkarni, C., Stone, M., & Heer, J. (2013). Selecting semantically-resonant colors for data visualization. Computer Graphics Forum (Proceedings of EuroVis), 32(3), 401-410.

entries.caveats: Some conventions reverse by market; for example, red marks rising prices in several East Asian stock markets (recalled from memory, not verified). The Jonauskaite study measured associations between colour words and emotions, so applying it to status colours is an inference.

entries.principle: Clutter and crowding slow search
entries.claim: As a display gains more varied colours, orientations and contrasts, it becomes harder for any one item to stand out, and search slows. Items closely surrounded by others also become hard to recognise outside the centre of gaze.
entries.mechanism: Clutter is a state in which the features of a display vary so much that an added item can no longer draw attention. Crowding is a limit of peripheral vision: objects closer together than a critical spacing cannot be recognised without looking straight at them. Both force more eye movements.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — reducing feature variety and protecting key items with space cuts the number of places a person must inspect
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited papers
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — important items are visible at a glance

designMoves: Limit the variety of colours, type sizes, weights and border styles within one view.
Remove lines, boxes and icons that neither group nor inform.
Leave clear space around the items that must be found first.
Use one consistent icon style and one consistent card style.
Move secondary detail behind a disclosure control (see progressive-disclosure-and-onboarding).
antiPatterns: Each card with its own colour, icon style and border.
Borders, shadows and background tints all used at once to separate items.
A key button hemmed in by badges, links and icons.

howToCheck.machine: Compute clutter proxies per viewport from a screenshot: compressed image bytes per pixel and edge density, plus counts of distinct colours, font sizes, font weights and border styles. Compare against the Template baseline; no absolute threshold exists.
howToCheck.human: Time a first-time user who looks for one named item, and compare two versions of the page.

evidence.strengthNote: Rosenholtz, Li and Nakano (2007, Journal of Vision) defined three clutter measures (Feature Congestion, Subband Entropy, Edge Density) and showed that they correlate with search performance in complex images; they note that colour variability matters and that image file size tracked their main measure. Whitney and Levi (2011) review crowding as a fundamental limit on object recognition across most of the visual field. The measures were validated on maps and search displays, not on web pages.

sources.citation: Rosenholtz, R., Li, Y., & Nakano, L. (2007). Measuring visual clutter. Journal of Vision, 7(2):17.
Whitney, D., & Levi, D. M. (2011). Visual crowding: A fundamental limit on conscious perception and object recognition. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 15(4), 160-168.

entries.caveats: Clutter is not the same as density: a dense, uniform, well-grouped table can score low on clutter and be fast to use (see density-organised). The proxies describe an image and know nothing about the user's task.

entries.principle: Organisation matters more than amount
entries.claim: How a display is organised predicts search time better than how much it shows. Sparse, well-grouped regions are searched first and faster, yet practised users can work faster on dense screens with no loss of accuracy.
entries.mechanism: People search a display group by group. The crowding around each item (local density), the clarity of groups and the predictability of positions set how fast each group is scanned. Practised users know where things are, so more information in view saves them navigation.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — good grouping lowers search effort at any density; raising density without structure raises it
effects.satisfaction: mixed — nurses rated dense and sparse screens alike; newcomers may prefer sparse layouts
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — predictable positions and clear groups, at any density

designMoves: Set density by audience and task: lower for browsing and first-time use, higher for tools that practised people use all day.
Put the most important content in the least crowded region of the view.
When raising density, keep grouping, alignment and stable positions.
Remove chrome (padding, decoration, repeated labels) before removing data.
Offer a density setting in tools used for long sessions.
antiPatterns: A uniform wall of items with no grouping.
A sparse layout that makes practised users page or scroll to compare values.
The assumption that more white space is always better.

howToCheck.machine: Compute a local-density map (elements or ink in a sliding window) and report its mean and spread, the number of groups and the group sizes. Check that elements the Prescription marks as key sit in lower-density regions. Compare with the Template's density target.
howToCheck.human: Test with the real audience: first-time users on a finding task and practised users on a repeated lookup task.

evidence.strengthNote: Tullis (1983, 1984) measured overall density, local density, grouping and layout complexity on 520 character displays and predicted search time (R-squared .51). Halverson and Hornof (2004) found with eye tracking that sparse word groups were searched first and faster; in that study sparse groups also used larger type, so density and size are confounded. A later paper (Tarling and Brumby) reports that people chose sparse regions first even when dense ones were quicker to search. Staggers (1993) tested 110 clinical nurses: high-density screens gave faster target finding than moderate or low density, with the same accuracy and satisfaction (findings confirmed from the abstract of the underlying dissertation). All of this is old and uses text displays.

sources.citation: Tullis, T. S. (1983). The formatting of alphanumeric displays: A review and analysis. Human Factors, 25(6), 657-682.

Halverson, T., & Hornof, A. J. (2004). Local density guides visual search: Sparse groups are first and faster. Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting, 48. DOI 10.1177/154193120404801615.
Staggers, N. (1993). Impact of screen density on clinical nurses' computer task performance and subjective screen satisfaction. International Journal of Man-Machine Studies, 39(5), 775-792.

Tarling and Brumby (first names and year not confirmed). Density guides visual search: Sparse groups are first even when slower. Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting.

entries.caveats: The Staggers result applies to practised users on lookup tasks with well-organised screens; it does not license crowding a marketing page. Density measured in characters on text terminals does not translate directly to modern graphical layouts.

entries.principle: White space and comprehension: thin, mixed evidence
entries.claim: Evidence that white space around text improves comprehension is thin and mixed: one small study found slower reading but better comprehension with page margins, and a follow-up found only higher satisfaction. The often-quoted figure that white space raises comprehension by 20% could not be traced to a verified study.
entries.mechanism: Margins separate the text block from its surroundings, which may reduce interference from neighbouring content. The proposed mechanism is the same crowding and grouping described in other entries; nobody has measured it directly for margins.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — one small study suggests a comprehension benefit and one finds none
effects.satisfaction: raises — both studies found that readers were more satisfied with margined or better-spaced layouts
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Give text blocks side padding so that text never touches a container or screen edge.
Use space mainly to group and separate (see proximity-and-common-region), not as a general comprehension aid.
Expect a comfort and satisfaction benefit from adequate margins; do not promise a measured comprehension gain.
antiPatterns: Quoting '20% better comprehension from white space' as a research finding.
Text flush against the edge of a card or viewport.
Uniform extra padding everywhere, which removes grouping.

howToCheck.machine: Measure the padding between text blocks and the edges of their containers and of the viewport; flag zero or near-zero values.
howToCheck.human: Ask readers which of two versions is more comfortable to read; that is the outcome the evidence supports.

evidence.strengthNote: Chaparro, Baker, Shaikh, Hull and Brady (2004) compared four layouts that varied margins and line spacing: margins affected reading speed and comprehension, readers were more satisfied with margins, and line spacing changed preference only. The direction of the margin effect (slower reading, better comprehension) is recalled from the abstract; the search result confirmed only that both measures were affected. Chaparro, Shaikh and Baker (2005) found no effect of layout quality on speed or comprehension, only on satisfaction and reported fatigue. Both appeared in a university laboratory newsletter, not a peer-reviewed journal, and sample sizes were not confirmed. The '20%' figure circulates in design articles, usually credited to a 2004 study; it could not be verified and has grade D.

sources.citation: Chaparro, B., Baker, J. R., Shaikh, A. D., Hull, S., & Brady, L. (2004). Reading online text: A comparison of four white space layouts. Usability News, 6(2).
Chaparro, B. S., Shaikh, A. D., & Baker, J. R. (2005). Reading online text with a poor layout: Is performance worse? Usability News, 7(1).

entries.caveats: The absence of strong evidence is not evidence that margins are useless; grouping and line-length effects are better supported and usually call for space anyway.

entries.principle: Generous white space signals quality by convention
entries.claim: Generous empty space around a product or message signals quality and prestige to viewers. The signal is a learned convention from twentieth-century art and advertising, not an inherent property of empty space.
entries.mechanism: Minimalist art, modern architecture and upscale corporate advertising linked empty space with restraint and expense. Viewers who have seen that pairing read empty space as a mark of a confident, high-end sender, even without knowing the history.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the effect concerns impression, not effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — perceived quality and prestige rise for audiences who share the convention; satisfaction with use was not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; the effect concerns impression

designMoves: Use generous space when the positioning is premium or calm, and pair it with restraint in colour and type.
Do not spend the space where it costs working efficiency, such as in dense tools.
Check that the audience shares the convention.
antiPatterns: A vast, empty first screen on a tool that people open to find data.
A crowded layout for a brand that claims exclusivity.

howToCheck.machine: Report the share of the first viewport that contains no text, image or control, and compare it with the Template's target.
howToCheck.human: Ask a few people from the audience to describe the brand after a five-second view.

evidence.strengthNote: Pracejus, Olsen and O'Guinn (2006, Journal of Consumer Research) trace the history of the convention and report that creative directors at advertising agencies and ordinary consumers read white space in the same way. Later citing work credits the paper with the finding that surrounding a product with empty space raises its perceived prestige. The context is North American print advertising. This entry overlaps with the aesthetics and trust part of the knowledge base.

sources.citation: Pracejus, J. W., Olsen, G. D., & O'Guinn, T. C. (2006). How nothing became something: White space, rhetoric, history, and meaning. Journal of Consumer Research, 33(1), 82-90.

entries.caveats: A convention can change and can differ between cultures and sectors. Space that signals quality on a brand page can read as waste in a working tool.

entries.principle: Motion captures attention, and costs it
entries.claim: Movement at the edge of vision is detected more reliably than a change of colour or shape, and it distracts from the task at hand. Motion is therefore a strong and costly signal that should be reserved for things that need attention now.
entries.mechanism: Peripheral vision resolves little detail but is sensitive to movement and sudden appearance. Both pull attention without a decision by the viewer, who must then find their place in the task again.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — removing needless motion removes involuntary interruptions
effects.satisfaction: raises — the cited study treats irritation as a side effect of motion to be minimised
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — when only important events move, movement means something

designMoves: Reserve motion for events that need attention now, such as a new message, an error or a finished job.
Keep attention-getting motion brief and make it stop by itself.
Keep looping animation, autoplaying video and animated images away from text that people read and forms that people fill in.
Give anything that moves for more than five seconds beside other content a control to pause, stop or hide it (WCAG 2.2.2, Level A).
Use a quiet, static cue for status that does not need immediate attention.
antiPatterns: A looping background video behind hero text.
A badge that pulses until clicked.
An animated illustration beside a form.
Blinking text.

howToCheck.machine: List CSS animations with infinite iteration, autoplaying video and animated images. Flag any that run longer than five seconds without a pause control, and any inside or next to form and reading regions.
howToCheck.human: Read a paragraph on the page while each animation runs and note every time the eyes are pulled away.

evidence.strengthNote: Bartram, Ware and Calvert (2003, International Journal of Human-Computer Studies) found that moving icons were often better detected and identified than colour and shape codes, especially in the periphery, and that types of motion differ in how much they distract; the paper ends with guidelines for limiting distraction and irritation. The W3C explanation of criterion 2.2.2 states that moving content can be a severe distraction for some people, notably people with attention deficits, and that five seconds is long enough to get attention. The criterion text and the explanation were read.

sources.citation: Bartram, L., Ware, C., & Calvert, T. (2003). Moticons: Detection, distraction and task. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 58(5), 515-545.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide, Level A.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide.

entries.caveats: The strength that makes motion distracting also makes it the right tool for a rare, urgent alert. Which kinds of motion distract least was studied with small icons on desktop screens, and the detailed ranking was not confirmed here.

entries.principle: Change blindness: unattended changes go unseen
entries.claim: People often fail to notice a visible change on screen when it happens during an interruption, such as a page reload or a flash, or away from where they are looking. Even large changes can go unseen.
entries.mechanism: Seeing a change needs attention on the changing object at the moment of change. Normally the brief motion signal of a change attracts attention. A reload, blank frame or eye movement masks that signal, so the person can compare only against memory, which holds very little.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — feedback at the point of attention removes the need to hunt for what changed
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited study
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — each action has a visible consequence

designMoves: Show the result of an action at the place of the action, where the person is already looking.
When something elsewhere changes (a total, a cart count, a saved status), animate or briefly highlight that element.
Update the page in place; avoid a full reload for a small change.
Keep new or changed content marked for a few seconds.
Announce important updates to assistive technology with a live region.
antiPatterns: An error list at the top of a long form while the user looks at the submit button at the bottom.
A total that changes silently after an option is selected.
A brief notification in a far corner of a large screen.

howToCheck.machine: For each scripted action, measure the distance between the trigger and the region that changes. Flag changes that are off-screen or far from the trigger and have neither a transition or highlight nor a live-region announcement. Flag full document reloads after in-page actions. Report how long transient messages stay visible.
howToCheck.human: After each action, ask a test user what changed on the screen.

evidence.strengthNote: Rensink, O'Regan and Clark (1997, Psychological Science) introduced the flicker method: changes that were large, repeated and expected were extremely hard to notice when a brief blank separated two versions of a picture, and the authors conclude that attention is required to perceive change. The effect has been replicated many times with pictures and real-world scenes. Varakin, Levin and Fidler (2004) review the implications for interface design; that paper is cited from memory.

sources.citation: Rensink, R. A., O'Regan, J. K., & Clark, J. J. (1997). To see or not to see: The need for attention to perceive changes in scenes. Psychological Science, 8(5), 368-373.

Varakin, D. A., Levin, D. T., & Fidler, R. (2004). Unseen and unaware: Implications of recent research on failures of visual awareness for human-computer interface design. Human-Computer Interaction, 19(4), 389-422.

entries.caveats: Laboratory demonstrations use photographs and an artificial flicker; the interface equivalents are reloads, closing dialogs and scroll jumps. People also overestimate how well they notice changes, so teams tend to trust small notifications too much.

entries.principle: Transitions: short, purposeful, slow-in and slow-out
entries.claim: A short animated transition helps people keep track of what moved or changed between two states, and movement that starts slowly, speeds up and ends slowly is the easiest to follow. Animation used as an explanation rarely beats a good static picture.
entries.mechanism: A transition lets the viewer follow an object from the old state to the new one, so they do not have to find and identify it again after a jump. A slow start gives time to pick up the movement and a slow end makes the destination predictable. Long or complex animation exceeds what a person can track and delays the next action.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — objects are followed, not re-identified
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the cited experiments measured tracking and estimation accuracy
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the relation between the two states is visible

designMoves: Animate changes that would otherwise be a jump: reordering, expanding, moving between levels.
Use an ease-in-out timing curve for objects that move between two on-screen positions.
Keep interface transitions short; practitioner guidance puts most of them between about 100 and 500 ms.
Move one thing at a time, or move related things together in the same direction.
Never block input until an animation ends.
antiPatterns: Linear, constant-speed movement for objects.
Page transitions that last a second or more.
Many elements moving in different directions at once.
Entrance animations on every scroll for decoration.

howToCheck.machine: List CSS transitions and animations with their duration and timing function per property. Flag durations above the Catalog maximum, linear timing on position or size changes, and animations during which the page ignores input.
howToCheck.human: After a transition, ask the viewer where an item went. A wrong or slow answer means the transition did not do its job.

evidence.strengthNote: Heer and Robertson (2007) ran two controlled experiments in which animated transitions between chart types improved object tracking and value estimation. Dragicevic, Bezerianos, Javed, Elmqvist and Fekete (CHI 2011) compared constant speed, slow-in/slow-out, fast-in/fast-out and an adaptive scheme for tracking moving points; slow-in/slow-out was best overall, though constant speed did better for some transition types (result confirmed through a later paper by the first author and through the authors' slides, not the paper text). Tversky, Morrison and Betrancourt (2002) reviewed animation for teaching and found that benefits often vanished when the static version carried the same information (secondary summaries). The duration range is practitioner guidance from Nielsen Norman Group, recalled from memory, with grade C.

sources.citation: Heer, J., & Robertson, G. (2007). Animated transitions in statistical data graphics. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 13(6), 1240-1247.
Dragicevic, P., Bezerianos, A., Javed, W., Elmqvist, N., & Fekete, J.-D. (2011). Temporal distortion for animated transitions. Proceedings of CHI 2011, 2009-2018.
Tversky, B., Morrison, J. B., & Betrancourt, M. (2002). Animation: Can it facilitate? International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 57(4), 247-262.

entries.caveats: The tracking studies used moving points in data graphics; ordinary interface transitions are simpler. Frequent, repeated actions by practised users are often better with no animation. All motion must respect the reduced-motion setting (see reduced-motion).

entries.principle: Motion can make people ill: respect reduced motion, never flash
entries.claim: Some people become dizzy or nauseous from on-screen motion such as parallax, zooming and large moving areas, and flashing content can trigger seizures. Standards forbid more than three flashes per second, require a pause control for long-running motion and, at the strictest level, require that motion triggered by interaction can be switched off.
entries.mechanism: The balance system of the inner ear (the vestibular system) reports that the body is still while the eyes report movement; in sensitive people the conflict causes dizziness, nausea and headache. In photosensitive epilepsy, flashes that are large, bright and faster than about three per second can start a seizure.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — for affected users, who can keep working without symptoms
effects.satisfaction: raises — for affected users; unmeasured for others
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; a correctly reduced interface keeps the same behaviour without the movement

designMoves: Honour the prefers-reduced-motion setting: replace movement with a fade or an instant change.
Keep state changes and feedback when motion is reduced; remove the movement, not the information.
Do not make parallax, scroll-linked movement or large zooming and panning the default for essential content.
Never show content that flashes more than three times in one second.
Provide pause, stop or hide for anything that moves for more than five seconds.
antiPatterns: Scroll-driven effects with no off switch.
Ignoring the operating-system reduce-motion setting.
Removing all feedback, not only the movement, when reduced motion is on.
Flashing banners or strobe-like video.

howToCheck.machine: Emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce and assert that no transform-based or scroll-linked animation runs while state changes still appear. Analyse animations and video frames for more than three luminance flashes in any second. Detect motion longer than five seconds with no pause control.
howToCheck.human: Turn on the operating-system reduce-motion setting and use the whole product.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criteria 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A), 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) and 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (Level AAA) were read from the W3C source repository, with their explanations; the explanation for 2.3.3 describes dizziness, nausea and headaches and names parallax, but cites no research. The MDN reference for prefers-reduced-motion was read. Prevalence context: Agrawal and colleagues (2009) found vestibular dysfunction, measured by a balance test, in 35.4% of 5,086 US adults aged 40 and over.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold, Level A.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions, Level AAA.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 2.3.3: Animation from Interactions.
MDN Web Docs. prefers-reduced-motion media feature reference.

Agrawal, Y., Carey, J. P., Della Santina, C. C., Schubert, M. C., & Minor, L. B. (2009). Disorders of balance and vestibular function in US adults: Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2001-2004. Archives of Internal Medicine, 169(10), 938-944.

entries.caveats: The 35.4% figure counts people who failed a balance test, not people who are sickened by screen motion; nobody has measured the second number. Evidence about which web effects trigger symptoms is clinical experience and self-report. Criterion 2.3.3 is Level AAA, so most legal regimes do not require it, but honouring the setting costs little.

entries.principle: Auto-rotating carousels hide content and distract
entries.claim: An auto-rotating carousel hides most of its content most of the time, is often taken for advertising, and moves while people try to read. In usability testing, users failed to find prominent content that sat in a rotating carousel.
entries.mechanism: Three effects combine: the movement pulls attention and takes control of reading time away from the reader, the banner-like look triggers the habit of skipping advertising, and only one panel is visible at any moment.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a static presentation removes movement and the need to wait for or chase a panel
effects.satisfaction: raises — the practitioner article reports that auto-forwarding annoys users
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — all key content is visible and stays where it is

designMoves: Put the single most important message in a static hero.
If several messages matter, show them together, for example in a grid, or choose one.
If a carousel is required, do not advance it automatically; otherwise provide a pause control and stop on hover, on focus and after any interaction.
Give the carousel visible, labelled controls and make every slide reachable by keyboard.
antiPatterns: A home-page slider that changes every few seconds.
A carousel used to avoid deciding which message has priority.
Tiny dots as the only controls.

howToCheck.machine: Detect elements whose visible child changes on a timer. Assert that a pause control exists, that rotation stops on hover, on focus and after interaction, and that every slide can be reached by keyboard.
howToCheck.human: Ask a test user to find information that sits on the third slide.

evidence.strengthNote: Nielsen Norman Group (2013) reports a usability study in which users could not find content shown prominently in an auto-rotating carousel; the article was seen only through secondary summaries. Analytics from one university site, published by Runyon in 2013 and recalled from memory, showed that about 1% of visitors clicked a carousel item, mostly on the first slide. WCAG 2.2.2 (Level A) requires a pause mechanism for such motion. The evidence is practitioner-level and partly from single sites.

sources.citation: Nielsen, J. (2013). Auto-Forwarding Carousels and Accordions Annoy Users and Reduce Visibility. Nielsen Norman Group.
Runyon, E. (2013). Carousel interaction stats (analytics from the University of Notre Dame website). Author's blog.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide, Level A.

entries.caveats: User-controlled carousels, such as a product image gallery that the user swipes, are a different pattern and are widely accepted. The click data come from one site and say nothing about whether people saw the first slide.

entries.principle: Every field needs a visible, persistent label
entries.claim: Every input needs a visible label that stays visible while the person types and afterwards. Placeholder text inside the field is not a label: it disappears on input, strains memory, is often too faint, and can be mistaken for a value that is already filled in.
entries.mechanism: The label is the cue that says what to enter. When it vanishes, the person must recall it, and a completed form can no longer be checked without emptying fields. Faint placeholder text also fails contrast requirements.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the cue stays on screen, so nothing has to be recalled
effects.satisfaction: raises — forms rebuilt to follow such guidelines were rated higher in a controlled study
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — each field says what it wants

designMoves: Give every field a visible text label outside the field, connected to it in code.
Place the label above the field as the default; this also works on narrow screens.
Put hints and format examples as text between the label and the field, not in the placeholder.
State in text which fields are optional or required.
Size each field to the length of the expected answer.
antiPatterns: A field whose only description is its placeholder.
Grey placeholder text that carries instructions.
An icon as the only label of a field.

howToCheck.machine: For each input, assert a programmatically associated label and a visible text label outside the input that remains visible when the field holds a value. Flag inputs described only by a placeholder attribute, and compute placeholder contrast.
howToCheck.human: Fill in the form, then try to review every answer without clicking into any field.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criterion 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A) was read; its explanation says labels must be persistently available. The GOV.UK Design System guidance (read) forbids placeholders in place of labels or hints. Nielsen Norman Group (Sherwin 2014) lists the usability problems of placeholders. Label position has only small, conflicting studies: Penzo (2006, informal eye tracking on a four-field form) favoured labels above fields, while Das and McEwan (2008) found right-aligned labels fastest, then top, then left. Seckler and colleagues (CHI 2014, 65 participants) showed that forms improved with 20 guidelines together were completed faster, with fewer submission attempts and higher satisfaction.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions, Level A, with its Understanding document.
GOV.UK Design System. Text input component guidance.
Sherwin, K. (2014). Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful. Nielsen Norman Group.
Seckler, M., Heinz, S., Bargas-Avila, J. A., Opwis, K., & Tuch, A. N. (2014). Designing usable web forms: Empirical evaluation of web form improvement guidelines. Proceedings of CHI 2014.
Das, S., & McEwan, T. (2008). Using eye-tracking to evaluate label alignment in online forms.

entries.caveats: The W3C explanation accepts that a visible label is not always necessary, for example for a search field with a clear icon and button. The above-the-field position is a sound convention, not a strong research finding. The Seckler study tested 20 guidelines together, so it cannot credit any single one.

entries.principle: Validate after the user finishes, not while they type
entries.claim: Show a validation error only after the person has finished with a field or has submitted the form, never during a first attempt at typing. Remove the error as soon as the input becomes valid.
entries.mechanism: An error that appears mid-entry interrupts the person and reports a mistake they have not yet made, which forces a switch from entering to correcting. Feedback after completion arrives when the person is ready to review.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no interruptions during entry and a clear moment for correction
effects.satisfaction: raises — participants rated forms with after-field validation about 31% higher in a small practitioner test
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the form reacts when the person expects it to

designMoves: Validate a field when the person leaves it, or validate the form on submit.
Never show an error on the first keystrokes of a first attempt.
Once an error is showing, re-check on each keystroke so that it clears the moment the input is valid.
Place the message next to its field; after a failed submit, add a summary at the top that links to each field.
Keep everything the person typed.
antiPatterns: 'Invalid email address' after the first character.
Errors shown only in an alert box.
An error that stays after the input has been corrected.

howToCheck.machine: Script each field: type the first character of a valid value and assert that no error appears; leave the field with an invalid value and assert that an error appears next to it and is linked in code; correct the value and assert that the error disappears without resubmitting; submit with errors and assert that focus moves to the summary or the first error.
howToCheck.human: Watch a first-time user complete the form and note every moment at which a message interrupts typing.

evidence.strengthNote: Bargas-Avila, Oberholzer, Schmutz, de Vito and Opwis (2007, Interacting with Computers) ran two studies with 77 and 90 participants and concluded that errors are best shown after the user completes the form, and that immediate feedback performed worst (from a catalogue abstract and a truncated excerpt). Wroblewski (2009), with the usability firm Etre, tested 22 users on six versions of a registration form: validation after each field cut completion time by about 42% and errors by about 22% compared with validation on submit only, and validation before or during typing was the worst variant. The two studies disagree on whether after-field beats after-submit; both find during-typing worst. Both used short registration forms.

sources.citation: Bargas-Avila, J. A., Oberholzer, G., Schmutz, P., de Vito, M., & Opwis, K. (2007). Usable error message presentation in the World Wide Web: Do not show errors right away. Interacting with Computers, 19(3), 330-341.
Wroblewski, L. (2009). Inline Validation in Web Forms. A List Apart.

entries.caveats: Immediate feedback is useful for a few fields where the person wants guidance while typing, such as a password-strength hint or a check that a username is free. The percentages come from one small practitioner test and should not be quoted as general effect sizes.

entries.principle: Errors: identify, explain, and allow recovery
entries.claim: When input is wrong, the interface must say in text which item has the problem and how to fix it. For submissions that create legal or financial commitments or change the user's data, it must let the user check, confirm or undo.
entries.mechanism: A person can correct only what they can locate and understand. Generic or colour-only errors leave them searching and guessing. Review and undo steps catch slips, which are errors of execution that the person would recognise if shown.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the message removes the search for what went wrong and how to fix it
effects.satisfaction: raises — government service testing found that users recovered from errors with messages written this way
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the form explains itself when something goes wrong

designMoves: Write each error as a specific instruction that names the field and the fix, such as 'Enter a date after today'.
Show the message next to the field and in a summary; never signal an error by colour alone.
Use plain words and avoid blame, jargon and codes.
Keep all entered data when showing errors.
For legal, financial and data-changing submissions, provide a review step, a confirmation or an undo.
Warn before a session expires and let the person extend it.
antiPatterns: 'An error occurred' or 'Invalid input'.
A red border as the only error signal.
A form that empties itself on error.
An irreversible action with neither confirmation nor undo.

howToCheck.machine: Submit each form empty and with bad data. Assert that every invalid field has a text error, an invalid state in code and a link from the summary, and that values are preserved. Flag generic message strings from a list. For flows that the Prescription marks as legal, financial or destructive, assert a review, confirmation or undo step.
howToCheck.human: Read each error message alone and ask whether it tells a first-time user what to do next.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criteria 3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A), 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (Level AA), 3.3.4 Error Prevention for legal, financial and data submissions (Level AA) and 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A) were read from the W3C source repository. The GOV.UK Design System guidance on error messages (read) reports that messages written to its rules were tested with all types of users in live services and that users understood what went wrong and how to fix it; it gives no numbers.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.1 Error Identification, Level A.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.3 Error Suggestion, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data), Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, Level A.
GOV.UK Design System. Error message component guidance.

entries.caveats: Criterion 3.3.3 exempts suggestions that would weaken security, for example revealing whether the user name or the password was wrong. Confirmation dialogs lose force when they appear routinely, so undo is the better tool for frequent, reversible actions (a practitioner observation, not verified here).

entries.principle: Ask only for what is needed; keep the layout simple
entries.claim: Asking only for necessary information reduces abandonment: checkout research reports that a notable share of shoppers give up because the process is too long or complicated, and that typical checkouts show more fields than they need. Evidence for layout rules such as one column or one question per page is weaker and mixed.
entries.mechanism: Each field costs reading, recall, typing and a chance of error, and a long form signals high effort before the person starts. A single column gives one unambiguous reading order.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer decisions and one clear path through the form
effects.satisfaction: raises — complexity is among the reasons shoppers give for abandoning checkout
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the person can see what is asked and why
