designMoves: Remove every field that has no stated use; keep a written reason for each question.
Hide rarely used fields, such as a second address line or a company name, behind a link.
Lay out ordinary forms in one column.
For complex or unfamiliar transactions, ask about one topic per page; group several questions on a page for trained staff who repeat the task.
Explain why any sensitive or unexpected question is asked.
antiPatterns: A phone number requested 'just in case'.
Fields in several columns with an unclear reading order.
One very long page for a complex application.
A three-field form spread over three pages.

howToCheck.machine: Count visible fields per form and per step. List fields that are marked neither required nor optional. Detect inputs that share a row without being parts of one value such as a date. Count the steps.
howToCheck.human: For each field, ask the product owner what is done with the answer. Fields without an answer are candidates for removal.

evidence.strengthNote: Baymard Institute checkout research, as reported in search summaries of its 2024 article: the average checkout had 11.3 form fields, most sites need about 8, and about 17% of surveyed shoppers had abandoned an order because checkout was too long or complicated. Other Baymard benchmark years give different numbers. Layout has grade C: a CXL Institute test (2016, 702 participants) found a single-column form about 15 seconds faster than a multi-column one, while a HubSpot A/B test found a two-column form converting better. The GOV.UK Design System (read) recommends one question per page and asking only for needed information, without publishing data.

sources.citation: Baymard Institute (2024). Article on the average number of form fields in checkout flows. Baymard blog.
GOV.UK Design System. Question pages pattern guidance.
CXL Institute (2016). Form field usability study: single-column versus multi-column forms.
HubSpot. Disproving best practices: The one- vs. two-column form test.

entries.caveats: Field count stands in for effort; one hard question can cost more than three easy ones, and removing a field that users expect can hurt. The claim that every added field lowers conversion by a fixed percentage has no general basis. The shopper figures are survey self-reports from US e-commerce.

entries.principle: Defaults are powerful: choose them for the user
entries.claim: A pre-selected option is chosen far more often than the same option offered without pre-selection. Across 58 studies the average effect was large, but it varied widely and was sometimes negative.
entries.mechanism: The authors of the meta-analysis group the causes into three: people read a default as a recommendation, they treat it as the starting point from which change feels like a loss, and changing it takes effort.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a good default removes a decision
effects.satisfaction: mixed — a default that serves the user helps; a default that serves the business against the user damages trust
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the form arrives sensibly filled in

designMoves: Set each default to the safest and most common choice for the user.
Prefill what is already known and keep it editable.
Never pre-select options that benefit the business at the user's cost, such as paid add-ons or marketing consent.
Make defaults visible and easy to change.
Use no default where a deliberate choice matters, and require an active choice.
antiPatterns: A pre-ticked box for marketing email or an insurance add-on.
A privacy-relevant default buried in advanced settings.
The most expensive plan pre-selected.

howToCheck.machine: List every input that has a pre-selected value. Flag pre-checked boxes whose labels match patterns for consent, marketing, newsletters, add-ons, donations or upgrades.
howToCheck.human: For each default, ask whose interest it serves.

evidence.strengthNote: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber and Johnson (2019, Behavioural Public Policy) analysed 58 default studies with 73,675 participants in total: d = 0.68 (95% confidence interval 0.53 to 0.83), with substantial variation; two studies showed negative effects; defaults were more effective in consumer domains and less effective in environmental ones. Abstract confirmed.

sources.citation: Jachimowicz, J. M., Duncan, S., Weber, E. U., & Johnson, E. J. (2019). When and why defaults influence decisions: A meta-analysis of default effects. Behavioural Public Policy, 3(2), 159-186.

entries.caveats: Because defaults work, they carry an ethical and legal load. In the European Union a pre-ticked box is not valid consent (Court of Justice ruling in Planet49, 2019; recalled from memory, not verified). People who distrust the party that set a default may reject it.

entries.principle: Support autofill, paste and password managers
entries.claim: Inputs that collect information about the user must declare their purpose in code so that browsers and password managers can fill them (WCAG 1.3.5, Level AA). US federal guidance requires sites to allow password managers and autofill, and recommends allowing paste and offering an option to show the password.
entries.mechanism: Autofill replaces recall and typing with a quick confirmation, which removes typing errors and helps most on phones. A password manager lets a person use long, unique passwords without remembering them.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — nothing to recall and little to type
effects.satisfaction: unknown — plausible but unmeasured; the only speed figure is an unpublished vendor claim
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the form fills itself correctly

designMoves: Set a valid autocomplete value on every field for personal data: name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, cc-number, one-time-code, username, new-password, current-password.
Choose the input type and inputmode that bring up the right keyboard; use inputmode numeric for whole numbers.
Never block paste, in particular on password and one-time-code fields.
Offer a control that shows the password.
Impose no composition rules and no periodic change; accept passwords of at least 64 characters.
antiPatterns: autocomplete set to off on name, address or payment fields.
Paste disabled on a password field or a 'confirm email' field.
'Must contain an uppercase letter, a number and a symbol.'
A one-time code split across six boxes that reject paste.

howToCheck.machine: For each input that collects personal data, assert a valid autocomplete token and a suitable type and inputmode. Paste a value into password and one-time-code fields and assert that it is accepted. Assert a show-password control. Assert that a password maxlength is absent or at least 64. Flag text that states composition rules.
howToCheck.human: Complete sign-up and sign-in with a password manager on a phone.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criteria 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (both Level AA) were read. NIST Special Publication 800-63B-4 (final, 2025), section 3.1.1, was read from the NIST source repository: verifiers SHALL allow password managers and autofill, SHOULD permit paste, SHOULD offer an option to display the password, SHALL NOT impose composition rules, SHALL NOT require periodic change, SHALL require at least 15 characters for a password used alone and at least 8 when it is one factor of several, and SHOULD permit at least 64 characters. Only the first 100,000 characters of that page were read. The claim that correct autocomplete attributes make form completion 'up to 30% faster' is a 2015 statement by the Chrome team with no published method (grade C).

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), Level AA.
National Institute of Standards and Technology (2025). Special Publication 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, section 3.1.1 Passwords.
MDN Web Docs. HTML autocomplete attribute reference.
GOV.UK Design System. Text input component guidance.

entries.caveats: The NIST publication binds US federal systems and serves as a reference elsewhere. Criterion 1.3.5 covers fields about the user, not fields about other people. The GOV.UK guidance advises against input type number unless research shows a need.

entries.principle: Show a few options; do not hide them in a drop-down
entries.claim: When there are few options, show them all as radio buttons or checkboxes. Visible options are chosen more often than hidden ones, and government usability research found that many users struggle to operate drop-down lists.
entries.mechanism: A closed drop-down hides the choices until the person acts, so they cannot recognise the answer at a glance. Options that are visible at once get picked more. Drop-downs also demand fine control: opening, scrolling and telling the highlighted item from the selected one.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the choices can be read without an extra action
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the cited sources
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the question and its possible answers are visible together

designMoves: Use radio buttons for a small set of exclusive options and checkboxes for multiple choice.
Rephrase the question so that fewer options are needed.
For a long, familiar list such as countries, use a drop-down or a text field with suggestions.
Use text fields for dates of birth.
Do not use a multiple-selection list box.
antiPatterns: A drop-down for 'Yes' and 'No'.
A long drop-down with no way to type ahead.
A scrolling box that shows only part of a short list.

howToCheck.machine: Count select elements and their options. Flag selects with fewer options than the Catalog threshold (candidates for radio buttons), long selects with no type-ahead or search, and selects that allow multiple choices.
howToCheck.human: Watch first-time users on a phone operate each drop-down.

evidence.strengthNote: Couper, Tourangeau, Conrad and Crawford (2004) randomly assigned web-survey respondents to radio buttons, a closed drop box or a scrolling box that showed some options: options visible without action were endorsed more often, an effect the authors describe as stronger than order effects. The GOV.UK Design System guidance (read) reports research in which users could not close a select, tried to type into it, confused the focused option with the selected one, tried to pinch-zoom the options and did not realise they could scroll; it calls the select a last resort for public-facing services.

sources.citation: Couper, M. P., Tourangeau, R., Conrad, F. G., & Crawford, S. D. (2004). What they see is what we get: Response options for web surveys. Social Science Computer Review, 22(1), 111-127.
GOV.UK Design System. Select component guidance.

entries.caveats: The survey experiment shows that the control changes which answers people give, which matters for data quality as well as ease. Native drop-downs on phones open the system picker, which many people handle well. Radio buttons take more space.

entries.principle: Information scent: labels decide where people go
entries.claim: People choose a link by judging, from its label and surroundings, how likely it is to lead to what they want. Clear, specific labels keep people browsing; where labels are vague or menus are narrow, people fall back on site search, which does not make them faster or more accurate.
entries.mechanism: Information scent is a person's imperfect estimate of the value and cost of following a path, formed from nearby cues such as link text, icons and surrounding words. People follow the strongest scent and leave when it fades.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a specific label answers the question 'is it here?' before the click
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the cited experiments measured behaviour, speed and accuracy
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the site appears to be organised the way the user thinks

designMoves: Label navigation and links with the users' own words and with specific nouns or verbs, such as 'Pricing' or 'Track an order'.
Write link text that describes its destination when read alone.
Put the distinguishing words first.
Add a short description under any category name that could be misread.
Pair icons with text labels.
Provide search as a complement to navigation, not as a repair for it.
antiPatterns: 'Click here', 'Learn more', 'Solutions', 'Resources'.
Invented brand names for sections.
Icon-only navigation.
Relying on search to make up for unclear menus.

howToCheck.machine: Extract all link and button texts. Flag generic strings (click here, read more, learn more, here, more) that have no programmatic context, identical texts that point to different destinations, and icon-only navigation items.
howToCheck.human: Run a tree test: give users tasks and a text-only version of the menu, and record where they go first.

evidence.strengthNote: Pirolli and Card (1999, Psychological Review) set out information foraging theory with a rational analysis and a process model. Katz and Byrne (2003, ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction) found in e-commerce experiments that menu breadth and scent both influenced browsing, that site search did not yield faster or more accurate product finding, and that search should not be used to compensate for poor menus; secondary summaries report search on fewer than 10% of trials with broad, well-labelled menus and on almost 40% with narrow, vague ones. WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose (Level A) and 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA) were read.

sources.citation: Pirolli, P., & Card, S. (1999). Information foraging. Psychological Review, 106(4), 643-675.
Katz, M. A., & Byrne, M. D. (2003). Effects of scent and breadth on use of site-specific search on e-commerce Web sites. ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 10(3), 198-220.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), Level A.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Labels, Level AA.

entries.caveats: Scent depends on the audience: a label that is clear to staff can mean nothing to customers, so labels must be tested with real users. People who know the exact name of an item often prefer search, especially in very large catalogues.

entries.principle: Prefer broad, shallow navigation to deep, narrow navigation
entries.claim: For the same content, a structure with more options per level and fewer levels is usually faster and causes fewer wrong turns than a deep, narrow one, provided that the options on each level are grouped and clearly labelled. Extremely broad single levels lose the advantage.
entries.mechanism: Each level is a decision made under uncertainty about what a category contains, and upper-level categories are the vaguest. Every extra level adds a chance of a wrong turn. Scanning a longer, grouped, visible list costs little by comparison, because nothing has to be remembered.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer uncertain decisions on the way to a destination
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not confirmed from the cited abstract
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — destinations are visible early

designMoves: Prefer two levels of well-labelled options to four levels of few options.
Group the items of a broad level under headings.
Use concrete names for top-level categories.
Link popular deep pages directly from the top level.
Do not cap the number of items per level at seven (see miller-seven-misreading).
antiPatterns: A deep tree with three or four vague choices at each level.
Hub pages that only link onward.
Removing menu items to meet a quota.

howToCheck.machine: Build the navigation tree from the menus and the sitemap. Report maximum and mean depth, items per level and clicks to each destination. Flag destinations deeper than the Catalog limit and levels with very few options that only lead onward.
howToCheck.human: Run a tree test on the proposed structure and compare first-click success between a broad and a deep version.

evidence.strengthNote: Larson and Czerwinski (CHI 1998) arranged 512 items in three structures (8 by 8 by 8, 16 by 32 and 32 by 16): the three-level structure performed worst and a two-level structure of medium breadth did best. Earlier menu experiments from the 1980s point the same way (recalled from memory, not checked). These are small laboratory studies with text links; no recent large replication on modern sites was found.

sources.citation: Larson, K., & Czerwinski, M. (1998). Web page design: Implications of memory, structure and scent for information retrieval. Proceedings of CHI 1998, 25-32.

entries.caveats: The advantage of breadth depends on the quality of grouping and labels. Small screens limit breadth, so phones often need one more level. A broad level without grouping turns into a long unordered list.

entries.principle: Keep the main navigation visible when there is room
entries.claim: Hiding the main navigation behind a menu button roughly halves how often people use it and makes tasks slower and harder, on desktop screens most of all.
entries.mechanism: Options that are out of sight are not considered, because recognition needs something to recognise. A hidden menu also gives no scent about what the site contains and adds a step.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the available destinations are visible without an extra action
effects.satisfaction: raises — participants rated tasks as easier with visible navigation
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the structure of the site is visible on arrival

designMoves: On wide screens, show the main navigation as visible, labelled links.
On phones, show the few most important destinations directly and put the rest behind a button.
Label the menu button with a word such as 'Menu', not only an icon.
Do not hide navigation on large screens for the sake of a clean look.
antiPatterns: A menu icon as the only navigation on a desktop layout.
An unlabelled icon button for the menu.
Search hidden inside the menu.

howToCheck.machine: At each breakpoint, assert that the primary navigation links are visible without interaction when the viewport is wider than the Catalog breakpoint. Where a menu button is used, assert a visible text label and an accessible name.
howToCheck.human: Ask first-time users to find a section that is reachable only through the menu, and record whether they open it.

evidence.strengthNote: Nielsen Norman Group (Pernice and Budiu 2016) ran a quantitative usability study on desktop and phone. On desktop, people used hidden navigation in 27% of cases against 48 to 50% for visible or combined navigation; the firm summarises the result as discoverability cut almost in half, with longer task times and higher perceived difficulty. A secondary source gives 179 participants. One practitioner study; familiarity with the menu icon has probably grown since 2015.

sources.citation: Pernice, K., & Budiu, R. (2016). Hamburger Menus and Hidden Navigation Hurt UX Metrics. Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: On phones some hiding is unavoidable; the study supports showing the top destinations, not showing everything. Tools with a single dominant task may not need persistent navigation.

entries.principle: Follow conventions and stay consistent
entries.claim: People arrive with expectations about where common page elements are and how they behave, learned from the other sites they use. Matching those expectations, and keeping navigation and naming the same from page to page, lets them find things without first learning this site.
entries.mechanism: Expectations direct attention: people look first where an element usually is. An element in an unexpected place is searched for in the wrong spot first. Consistency inside a site lets one learned location serve every page.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — learned locations and names are reused
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not confirmed from the cited abstract
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — 'intuitive' largely means 'works like what I already know'

designMoves: Place the standard elements where people expect them: logo at the top start linking to the home page, main navigation across the top or down the start side, search near the top, account and cart at the top end, contact and legal links in the footer.
Keep navigation in the same order and place on every page.
Give the same function the same name and icon everywhere.
Depart from a convention only for a tested reason.
antiPatterns: Navigation that changes order or position between pages.
New icons or playful names for standard functions.
A logo that does not link to the home page.

howToCheck.machine: Across a crawl, assert that navigation items appear in the same relative order on every page, that the logo sits at the start of the header and links to the home page, that search (if present) is in the header, and that components with the same function have the same accessible name on every page.
howToCheck.human: Ask first-time users where they would expect to find search, contact details and the account page before they see the design.

evidence.strengthNote: Roth, Schmutz, Pauwels, Bargas-Avila and Opwis (2010, Interacting with Computers) asked users where they expect common objects on online shops, news portals and company pages: users largely agreed on the location of many objects, across demographic groups (sample size not confirmed). WCAG 2.2 criteria 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation and 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (both Level AA) were read and make consistency within a site a formal requirement. The maxim that users spend most of their time on other sites ('Jakob's law') is a practitioner summary of this idea.

sources.citation: Roth, S. P., Schmutz, P., Pauwels, S. L., Bargas-Avila, J. A., & Opwis, K. (2010). Mental models for web objects: Where do users expect to find the most frequent objects in online shops, news portals, and company web pages? Interacting with Computers, 22(2), 140-152.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.4 Consistent Identification, Level AA.

entries.caveats: Expectations belong to a time, a culture and a type of site; the study is from 2010 and did not find agreement for every object. 'Start' and 'end' mean left and right in left-to-right languages and the reverse in right-to-left languages.

entries.principle: People scan first and read selectively
entries.claim: Most people scan a web page for words that match their goal and read only parts of the text. Text written for scanning (short, structured, plainly worded) measured far higher on usability than the same content as promotional prose.
entries.mechanism: Reading everything costs time, so people sample headings, first words and highlighted terms to decide where reading will pay off.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — structure lets readers skip what they do not need
effects.satisfaction: raises — the rewritten versions also scored higher on subjective measures in the original study (recalled from memory)
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the page shows its contents at a glance

designMoves: Write short paragraphs with one idea each.
Use subheadings that state the content of the section.
Turn parallel items into bulleted lists.
Highlight a few key terms.
Cut promotional filler and start with the conclusion.
antiPatterns: A wall of text.
Clever or teasing headings.
A long introduction before the point.
Quoting 'users read only 20% of a page' as an exact statistic.

howToCheck.machine: Per page, compute words per paragraph, sentences per paragraph, the share of text in lists and the number of headings per few hundred words. Flag paragraphs above the Catalog word limit and long text with no subheadings.
howToCheck.human: Give a reader ten seconds with the page, then ask what it is about and what they can do there.

evidence.strengthNote: All figures in this note are recalled from memory, because the search budget ran out before they could be re-checked. Nielsen (1997) reported that 79% of test users scanned any new page and 16% read word by word; Morkes and Nielsen (1997) measured 124% higher usability for a concise, scannable, objective rewrite. Famous but weak: 'users read at most 28% of the words, 20% is more likely' (Nielsen 2008) is a calculation from browsing logs of one small study of mostly academic users (Weinreich and colleagues 2008), using time on page and an assumed reading speed. It is a rough upper bound per page visit, not a measured law, and has grade D as a precise number. A Nielsen Norman Group eye-tracking article (seen in search results) states that reading on the web depends heavily on the task.

sources.citation: Nielsen, J. (1997). How Users Read on the Web. Nielsen Norman Group (Alertbox).
Morkes, J., & Nielsen, J. (1997). Concise, SCANNABLE, and Objective: How to Write for the Web.
Nielsen, J. (2008). How Little Do Users Read? Nielsen Norman Group (Alertbox).
Nielsen Norman Group. Text Scanning Patterns: Eyetracking Evidence.

entries.caveats: People read closely when the content matches a strong need, and long articles do get read. The advice fits informational and task pages. The 1997 studies are old and small by current standards, although later eye-tracking work by the same firm points the same way.

entries.principle: The F-pattern is a symptom of unstructured text, not a layout rule
entries.claim: The F-shaped scanning pattern, in which attention goes to the first lines and then down the starting edge, appears when text has no headings or other structure and the reader is not committed. It is one of several patterns, and good formatting replaces it with more effective scanning.
entries.mechanism: A reader starts at the top, reads across, loses interest, moves down, reads less of each line and finally skims the starting edge. When clear headings exist, readers jump from heading to heading and read beneath the ones that matter, which eye-tracking researchers call the layer-cake pattern.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — headings let readers reach the relevant part directly
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the sources seen
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the structure of the content is visible

designMoves: Break text with informative headings so that readers scan from heading to heading.
Put the key words first in headings, paragraphs and list items.
Put the most important information in the first two paragraphs.
Do not arrange a layout in the shape of an F.
antiPatterns: Placing calls to action along an 'F' because 'users read in an F'.
Long text with no subheadings.
Important information at the end of long lines deep in a text block.

howToCheck.machine: Flag text blocks longer than the Catalog limit that contain no subheading or list. Flag headings that begin with generic words such as 'Introduction' or 'More about'.
howToCheck.human: Read only the first three words of each line of a page. If the result means nothing, the page invites F-pattern skimming.

evidence.strengthNote: Nielsen Norman Group eye tracking: the pattern was described in 2006 (232 users, recalled from memory) and revisited by Pernice in 2017 in an article whose title calls it misunderstood. The firm's pages, seen in search results, say that the shape is rough and variable, that it is one of several scanning patterns, that reading depends on the task, and that the layer-cake pattern is the most effective way to scan. The full 2017 article was not read. Heat maps average over many people; individuals differ.

sources.citation: Pernice, K. (2017). F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (Even on Mobile). Nielsen Norman Group.
Nielsen, J. (2006). F-Shaped Pattern for Reading Web Content (original eye-tracking research). Nielsen Norman Group.
Nielsen Norman Group. Text Scanning Patterns: Eyetracking Evidence.

entries.caveats: In right-to-left languages the pattern is mirrored. The original observations came from text-heavy pages and search results of the 2000s; image-led and card-based pages produce other patterns.

entries.principle: Front-load: the top of the page and the first words do most of the work
entries.claim: Attention falls steeply from the top of a page downward: in one large eye-tracking analysis, people spent more than half of their viewing time above the fold and about three quarters within the first two screenfuls. The top of the page and the first words of each heading and paragraph must carry the main point.
entries.mechanism: Everyone sees the top. Each further scroll is a decision based on what has been seen so far. Scanning eyes catch the first words of a line, so those words decide whether the rest is read.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the main point is available without scrolling or searching
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the sources seen
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the page says at once what it is and what can be done there

designMoves: State in the first screen what the page is and what the person can do.
Write in inverted-pyramid order: conclusion first, detail after.
Write headings that state the point and begin with the informative words.
Use real heading elements in a correct hierarchy, so that the structure also exists in code.
Show that the page continues below the first screen (see figure-ground-closure).
antiPatterns: A first screen with a slogan and no statement of the offer.
Key information after a long introduction.
Bold paragraphs used in place of heading elements.

howToCheck.machine: Assert one top-level heading and no skipped heading levels (axe-core has rules for both). Assert that the top-level heading and either the primary action or the key statement fall inside the first viewport at common sizes. Flag bold paragraphs that act as headings.
howToCheck.human: Read only the first screen and the headings. They should give the full outline of the page.

evidence.strengthNote: The attention figures (57% of viewing time above the fold, 74% in the first two screenfuls) come from a Nielsen Norman Group eye-tracking analysis by Fessenden (2018) and are recalled from memory; they could not be re-checked. They are averages over many sites and tasks from one firm's data. WCAG 2.2 criteria 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA) and 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A) were read; they require descriptive headings and structure that is available in code.

sources.citation: Fessenden, T. (2018). Scrolling and Attention. Nielsen Norman Group.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Labels, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, Level A.

entries.caveats: People do scroll, especially on phones, when the top gives them a reason; long pages work when each screen promises more. The fold is not a fixed line: it differs with every device.

entries.principle: Plain language helps everyone, experts included
entries.claim: Plain wording, short sentences and common words help every reader, including experts, to understand faster. The accessibility standard asks for text that a person with lower-secondary education can read, or for a simpler version beside the original.
entries.mechanism: Familiar words are recognised faster than rare ones. A short sentence holds fewer items in working memory before its meaning resolves. Jargon makes the reader recall or look up a definition.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — less decoding per sentence
effects.satisfaction: raises — practitioner studies report that experts also prefer plain text (recalled from memory)
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — instructions can be followed at first reading

designMoves: Use the reader's words, and define each technical term at first use.
Write short sentences with one idea each, in the active voice.
Address the reader as 'you' and state the action first.
For content aimed at the general public, aim for a lower-secondary reading level, or add a plain summary.
Test comprehension with real readers; use a readability formula only as a flag.
antiPatterns: Legal or marketing jargon inside instructions.
Unexplained abbreviations.
Simplifying by removing information that the reader needs.

howToCheck.machine: Per page, compute a readability index (for example the Flesch-Kincaid grade), mean sentence length and the share of passive sentences. Flag pages above the Catalog target and terms from a jargon list. Treat the scores as flags, not verdicts.
howToCheck.human: Ask a member of the audience to read a passage and say in their own words what they must do.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criterion 3.1.5 Reading Level (Level AAA) was read. The other supports are recalled from memory and were not re-checked: the US Plain Writing Act of 2010 obliges federal agencies to write clearly; ISO 24495-1:2023 is an international plain-language standard; Nielsen Norman Group studies (Nielsen 2005 on lower-literacy users; Loranger 2017 on experts) report better task success and a preference for plain text across literacy levels. No meta-analysis was located in this search.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 3.1.5 Reading Level, Level AAA.
Loranger, H. (2017). Plain Language Is for Everyone, Even Experts. Nielsen Norman Group.
United States Congress (2010). Plain Writing Act of 2010, Public Law 111-274.
International Organization for Standardization (2023). ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language, Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines.

entries.caveats: Readability formulas count word and sentence length; they do not measure clarity and can be gamed. A specialist audience needs its own terms, defined once. Where legal precision demands exact wording, add a plain summary and keep the precise text.

entries.principle: Touch targets: 24 CSS pixels minimum, about 44 for comfort
entries.claim: Pointer targets must measure at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels or have equivalent spacing (WCAG 2.5.8, Level AA). The stricter level asks for 44 by 44 (2.5.5, Level AAA), which is close to platform guidance for touch.
entries.mechanism: A fingertip covers far more area than a mouse pointer and hides the target while touching it. Tremor, one-handed use and movement, such as riding a bus, add error. A small or crowded target leads to the wrong control being activated.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer slips to notice and correct
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the standard reports no satisfaction data
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — controls respond to the first tap

designMoves: Make every interactive target at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
Make primary and frequent touch targets at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels.
Where the visible mark is small, such as a 16-pixel icon, enlarge the tappable area with padding.
Space undersized targets so that a 24-pixel circle centred on each does not overlap another target.
Use larger targets for actions that are frequent, hard to undo, near a screen edge or part of a sequence.
antiPatterns: A tiny close icon.
A dense row of icon buttons.
A stack of text links with tight line spacing as the main phone navigation.
A tappable area that covers only the glyph.

howToCheck.machine: At a phone viewport (for example 375 CSS pixels wide), read the bounding box of every interactive element. Flag any box under 24 by 24 unless a 24-pixel circle centred on it intersects no other target or its circle. Report the share of primary actions under 44 by 44.
howToCheck.human: Operate the page with a thumb on a real phone, one-handed, and count the mis-taps.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criteria 2.5.8 (Level AA, new in version 2.2) and 2.5.5 (Level AAA) and their explanations were read. The explanation says that the working group reviewed research and guidelines, which mostly concern touch and suggest larger sizes, and chose 24 as a floor for all pointer types after reviewing target sizes on high-traffic sites. It lists, without summarising, a study of one-handed thumb use (Parhi, Karlson and Bederson 2006), which recommended thumb targets of roughly 9 to 10 mm (recalled from memory). Apple's 44-point and Android's 48-dp guidance are also recalled from memory.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA.
W3C (2023). Understanding Success Criterion 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum).
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA.
Parhi, P., Karlson, A. K., & Bederson, B. B. (2006). Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices. Proceedings of MobileHCI 2006, 203-210.

entries.caveats: A CSS pixel is not a physical length, so the same target differs in millimetres between devices. The criterion exempts links inside sentences, controls sized by the browser, and targets whose size is essential. 24 pixels is a legal floor, not a comfortable touch size.

entries.principle: Thumb reach: lower and central areas are easier, but grips vary
entries.claim: On a phone held in one hand, controls in the lower and central part of the screen are easier to reach than the top corners. People change grip constantly, so 'thumb zone' maps are rough guides, not measurements.
entries.mechanism: The area a thumb can cover depends on hand size, grip and phone size. Reaching a far corner needs a change of grip or the other hand, and the hand hides part of the screen while reaching.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the effect is physical effort and slips
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured in the sources recalled
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Put frequent and primary actions in the lower half of the phone screen or in a bottom bar.
Do not make a top corner the only place for the primary action on tall phones.
Place rare or destructive actions further from the resting thumb.
Do not assume the right hand; avoid layouts that work for one side only.
antiPatterns: The only 'Save' or 'Next' control in the top corner of a tall screen.
Justifying a layout with a static thumb-zone picture.
An edge swipe as the only way to perform a core action.

howToCheck.machine: At phone viewport sizes, report the vertical position of each primary action. Flag primary actions that exist only in the top corners of screens taller than the Catalog limit.
howToCheck.human: Use the product one-handed with each hand on a large phone, and note each change of grip.

evidence.strengthNote: Both sources are recalled from memory and were not re-checked. Hoober (2013) observed 1,333 people using phones in public: about 49% held the phone in one hand, 36% cradled it in one hand and touched with the other, and 15% used two hands. Bergstrom-Lehtovirta and Oulasvirta (CHI 2014) modelled the reachable area of the thumb from hand size and grip. The coloured thumb-zone diagrams in design articles are illustrations and not data. Phones have grown since 2013.

sources.citation: Hoober, S. (2013). How Do Users Really Hold Mobile Devices? UXmatters.
Bergstrom-Lehtovirta, J., & Oulasvirta, A. (2014). Modeling the functional area of the thumb on mobile touchscreen surfaces. Proceedings of CHI 2014.

entries.caveats: Platform conventions still place some controls at the top (for example, a back control), and people cope with them through system gestures. Tablets and two-handed use have different reach patterns.

entries.principle: Reflow, zoom, and no hover-only or gesture-only functions
entries.claim: Content must work at a width of 320 CSS pixels without scrolling in two directions, allow text to be enlarged to 200%, and never depend on hover, dragging or multi-finger gestures alone (WCAG 2.2, Levels A and AA).
entries.mechanism: People with low vision zoom in; a 1,280-pixel window at 400% zoom is 320 pixels wide. Lines that run off the screen force back-and-forth scrolling, which makes readers lose their place. Touch screens have no hover, and dragging or tracing a path is hard for people with tremor or with alternative pointing devices.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the W3C explanation says horizontal scrolling significantly increases physical and cognitive effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the standard reports no satisfaction data
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — every function is reachable by the simplest input

designMoves: Build layouts that reflow to one column at 320 CSS pixels; avoid fixed widths.
Do not disable pinch zoom in the viewport settings.
Make everything that appears on hover also available on focus and on tap, and make it dismissible, hoverable and persistent.
Give every drag action, such as reordering or a slider, a single-tap or button alternative.
Give every swipe, pinch or path gesture a single-tap alternative.
antiPatterns: Horizontal scrolling of the page at phone width.
A tooltip as the only source of necessary information.
Drag-only reordering or swipe-only deletion.
A viewport setting that blocks zoom.

howToCheck.machine: Render at 320 CSS pixels wide and assert that the document does not scroll horizontally, except inside elements marked as tables, maps or code. Parse the viewport meta tag and flag settings that disable or limit zoom. Enlarge text to 200% and detect clipping. For content shown on hover, assert that it also appears on focus or tap. Flag draggable elements with no button alternative.
howToCheck.human: Use the product at 400% browser zoom and on a phone with one finger only.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criteria 1.4.10 Reflow (AA), 1.4.4 Resize Text (AA), 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (AA), 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (A) and 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA) were read from the W3C source repository, with the explanation for Reflow. That explanation refers to a 2017 study of the overhead of horizontal scrolling without giving its figures.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.10 Reflow, Level AA, with its Understanding document.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures, Level A.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, Level AA.
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text, Level AA.

entries.caveats: Content that needs two dimensions, such as data tables, maps, diagrams and video, may scroll both ways. Gestures and dragging that are essential to a function, such as drawing, are exempt.

entries.principle: What helps beginners can slow experts (expertise reversal)
entries.claim: Guidance that helps beginners, such as step-by-step instructions and explanations, can slow people who already know the task. An interface for a mixed audience needs help that beginners can see and experts can skip.
entries.mechanism: A beginner lacks a mental model of the task, so guidance stands in for it. A practised person already has the model; guidance then repeats what they know, and they must still read it and reconcile it with their own knowledge.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — guidance lowers load for beginners and raises it for experts
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not confirmed in this search
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — beginners find guided flows clear; experts find them slow

designMoves: Make help optional and collapsible, and remember that a person dismissed it.
Offer a fast path, such as bulk actions and remembered settings, beside the guided path.
In tools that people use every day, favour density, stable positions and shortcuts.
In products that people use rarely, such as a legal intake or a tax form, treat every visit as a beginner's visit.
antiPatterns: A tutorial that is forced on every session.
A wizard as the only route for a daily task.
Removing all guidance because 'our users are experts'.

howToCheck.machine: Assert that onboarding panels and tips can be dismissed and that the dismissal persists across reloads. Assert that guided flows offer a skip or an express route.
howToCheck.human: Test with both first-time and practised users, and compare where each group slows down.

evidence.strengthNote: The expertise reversal effect was named by Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller (2003) on the basis of instructional experiments; the paper is cited from memory and was not re-checked, and the evidence concerns learning materials. In interfaces, the verified menu model of Cockburn, Gutwin and Greenberg (2007) has separate components for beginners (visual search) and experts (decision from memory) and for the transition between them, which supports designing for both states.

sources.citation: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The expertise reversal effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31.
Cockburn, A., Gutwin, C., & Greenberg, S. (2007). A predictive model of menu performance. Proceedings of CHI 2007, 627-636.

entries.caveats: Expertise is specific to a task and depends on how often a person does it, not on general technical skill. The benefit of guidance for beginners is better established than the harm to experts.

entries.principle: Progressive disclosure, and learning by doing
entries.claim: Showing the common options first and revealing advanced ones on request helps beginners learn faster with fewer errors. People learn an interface mainly by using it, and upfront tutorials help only when the product is complex.
entries.mechanism: Fewer visible choices mean fewer wrong paths for a beginner. People want to get their own task done, so they skip instructions and try things; help that appears at the moment of need fits that behaviour.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — beginners face fewer choices and fewer error states
effects.satisfaction: mixed — hiding features that people need frustrates them
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the first view shows only what the main task needs

designMoves: Show the few most-used controls and put the rest behind one clearly labelled step, such as 'More options'.
Never hide what most users need for the main task.
Let people start the real task at once.
Teach in context: informative empty states, inline hints and a tip at the first use of a feature.
Make any tour skippable and available again later.
antiPatterns: A five-screen introduction before first use.
An essential setting under 'Advanced'.
Disclosure inside disclosure.
A feature tour that lists everything.

howToCheck.machine: Per view, count the controls visible by default and those behind disclosure. Assert that disclosure controls have text labels. Assert that any onboarding sequence has a skip control and that the main task is reachable without finishing it.
howToCheck.human: Watch a first-time user for five minutes with no instructions, and note what they try first and where they get stuck.

evidence.strengthNote: All sources are recalled from memory and were not re-checked. Carroll and Carrithers (1984) gave beginners a 'training wheels' word processor with advanced functions blocked; they got started faster and spent less time recovering from errors. Andersen and colleagues (CHI 2012) tested tutorials on more than 45,000 players of three games; tutorials raised engagement only in the most complex game. Carroll and Rosson (1987) describe the 'paradox of the active user': people skip instruction because they want to get on with their work. Nielsen Norman Group describes progressive disclosure as a pattern.

sources.citation: Carroll, J. M., & Carrithers, C. (1984). Training wheels in a user interface. Communications of the ACM, 27(8), 800-806.
Andersen, E., O'Rourke, E., Liu, Y.-E., Snider, R., Lowdermilk, J., Truong, D., Cooper, S., & Popovic, Z. (2012). The impact of tutorials on games of varying complexity. Proceedings of CHI 2012.
Carroll, J. M., & Rosson, M. B. (1987). Paradox of the active user. In J. M. Carroll (Ed.), Interfacing Thought. MIT Press.
Nielsen, J. (2006). Progressive Disclosure. Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: A hidden feature is found less often (see visible-navigation), so disclosure trades findability for simplicity; choose what to hide from usage data. Games are not productivity software, so the tutorial result transfers only as a pattern.

entries.principle: Shortcuts speed up experts, but only if people find them
entries.claim: Keyboard shortcuts and other accelerators make frequent actions much faster for practised users, yet most people never switch to them unless the interface keeps showing them. Shortcuts made of single character keys must be possible to turn off or remap.
entries.mechanism: A learned shortcut replaces pointing and menu search with one remembered action. Switching methods costs a short dip in speed, and people who are busy with their work stay with a method that already works.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — lower for those who have learned them; learning them is an extra demand
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not confirmed in this search
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; shortcuts do not change the visible interface

designMoves: Offer shortcuts for frequent actions and follow platform conventions.
Show each shortcut beside its menu item and in its tooltip.
Offer a command palette (a search box for commands) as a bridge between browsing menus and remembering keys.
Never make a shortcut the only way to do something.
Let users turn off or remap single-key shortcuts, or activate them only when the relevant component has focus.
antiPatterns: Shortcuts that are documented nowhere in the interface.
Overriding standard browser or system shortcuts.
Single-letter shortcuts that fire while the user dictates or types elsewhere.

howToCheck.machine: Detect key handlers at document level for single printable characters; assert a setting to disable or remap them, or that they act only on focus. Check that menu items and tooltips expose their shortcuts.
howToCheck.human: Ask a practised user which shortcuts they use and how they learned them.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts (Level A) was read. The behavioural evidence is recalled from memory and was not re-checked: Lane, Napier, Peres and Sandor (2005) found that experienced users of a word processor mostly kept using menus and toolbars although keyboard shortcuts were faster; Cockburn, Gutwin, Scarr and Malacria (2014) review how interfaces can support the move from beginner to expert methods.

sources.citation: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts, Level A.

Lane, D. M., Napier, H. A., Peres, S. C., & Sandor, A. (2005). Hidden costs of graphical user interfaces: Failure to make the transition from menus and icon toolbars to keyboard shortcuts. International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, 18(2), 133-144.
Cockburn, A., Gutwin, C., Scarr, J., & Malacria, S. (2014). Supporting novice to expert transitions in user interfaces. ACM Computing Surveys, 47(2), Article 31.

entries.caveats: Shortcuts pay off only for frequent actions. Web applications share the keyboard with the browser and with assistive technology, so conflicts are likely. Touch devices need other accelerators, such as recent items, with a visible alternative for each.

entries.principle: Keep things where they are: spatial memory makes repeat use fast
entries.claim: People learn where things are, and that memory makes repeated use fast. Interfaces that reorder or move items automatically, even to promote frequent ones, tend to be slower than layouts that stay put.
entries.mechanism: With repetition, visual search gives way to a remembered position: the person moves to the place without reading. An automatic change of order invalidates that memory and forces a new search.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — position is remembered, so no search is needed
effects.satisfaction: raises — in the menu study recalled from memory, most participants preferred menus they controlled over menus that adapted by themselves
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the interface behaves predictably

designMoves: Keep the order and position of navigation, toolbars and menu items fixed across pages and sessions.
To promote recent or frequent items, add a separate 'Recent' area and leave the main order alone.
Let users arrange things themselves if order matters to them.
Keep relative positions across screen sizes as far as possible.
In a redesign, keep the positions of the most-used controls.
antiPatterns: Menus that reorder by frequency of use.
A home screen that reshuffles on each visit.
'Smart' toolbars that hide unused items.

howToCheck.machine: Load key pages repeatedly and across simulated sessions; assert identical order and position of navigation and toolbar items. Flag code that sorts menu items by usage or recency.
howToCheck.human: Ask a practised user to point to a control from memory before the screen is shown.

evidence.strengthNote: Cockburn, Gutwin and Greenberg (CHI 2007, abstract confirmed) model the shift from visual search to remembered location and validated the model on traditional menus, split menus and an adaptive 'morphing' design. Findlater and McGrenere (CHI 2004), recalled from memory and not re-checked, compared static, adaptive and user-adaptable menus and found the static menu faster than the adaptive one. These are small laboratory studies of menus.

sources.citation: Cockburn, A., Gutwin, C., & Greenberg, S. (2007). A predictive model of menu performance. Proceedings of CHI 2007, 627-636.
Findlater, L., & McGrenere, J. (2004). A comparison of static, adaptive, and adaptable menus. Proceedings of CHI 2004, 89-96.

entries.caveats: Additive help, such as search suggestions or a recent-items list that leaves the main layout untouched, does not carry this cost. Content feeds are expected to change; the rule concerns controls and navigation.
